t.6.70.1: Rāghava too, having heard that vast uproar of battle between the Rākṣasas and the forest-dwellers, spoke to Jāmbavant.
t.6.70.2: Gentle one, surely a most difficult deed has been accomplished by Hanumān, for a terrible and very great clash of weapons is heard.
t.6.70.3: Therefore go, O lord of the bears, surrounded by your own army, and quickly lend aid to that foremost of monkeys who is fighting.
t.6.70.4: Saying "So be it," the king of the bears, surrounded by his own army, went toward the western gate, where the monkey Hanūmān was.
t.6.70.5: Then the lord of the bears saw Hanūmān coming along the road, surrounded by monkeys who had fought in battle and were panting hard.
t.6.70.6: And Hanumān, seeing on the road that fearsome army of bears, risen up for battle and resembling dark blue clouds, held it back and turned away.
t.6.70.7: Having quickly come near to Rāma together with that army of monkeys, the greatly renowned one, grieving, spoke these words to Rāma.
t.6.70.8: While we were fighting in battle and looking on, he, Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa, slew the weeping Sītā.
t.6.70.9: Having seen her, I am dejected, my mind bewildered, O subduer of enemies; and so I have come to make known to you what has happened.
t.6.70.10: Hearing those words of his, Rāghava, stupefied with grief, then fell to the ground like a tree whose roots have been cut.
t.6.70.11: Seeing that godlike Rāghava fallen upon the ground, the foremost of the monkeys leapt up and rushed toward him from every side.
t.6.70.12: And they sprinkled him with waters fragrant with lotuses and lilies, him who was blazing and unbearable, like a fire suddenly risen up.
t.6.70.13: Then Lakṣmaṇa, deeply grieved, embraced him with both arms and spoke to the distraught Rāma words endowed with reason and purpose.
t.6.70.14: Dharma is useless, for it cannot protect you from misfortunes, though you stand on the auspicious path, noble and with your senses subdued.
t.6.70.15: Beings, both the unmoving and the moving, are perceptible, but dharma is not perceived in that way; therefore it does not exist. Such is my view.
t.6.70.16: Just as the unmoving world is manifest, so too is the moving world of the same kind; yet this matter is not fitting in that way, for one such as you does not come to ruin.
t.6.70.17: If adharma were something real, Rāvaṇa would go to hell, and you, who are endowed with dharma, would not meet with such a calamity.
t.6.70.18: Since misfortune is absent for him, while you have fallen into misfortune, how could one say that one would gain dharma through dharma and adharma through adharma?
t.6.70.19: If people who delight in unrighteousness were not joined with righteousness, then righteousness would belong to those who walk in righteousness, and likewise these others would meet with their own fruit.
t.6.70.20: Because wealth flourishes for those in whom unrighteousness is firmly established, while those whose nature is righteous are made to suffer, these two are therefore meaningless.
t.6.70.21: If evil-doers are slain through adharma, O Rāghava, then dharma is struck down by the deed of killing; and once it is itself struck down, whom will it slay?
t.6.70.22: Or else, it is by what has been ordained that this man is slain or slays another; it is Fate that is smeared by that sinful deed, not he.
t.6.70.23: O tormentor of foes, how can the highest be attained by means of dharma, whose power to counter misfortune is never seen, which is unmanifest and, in truth, non-existent?
t.6.70.24: If righteousness truly existed, O foremost of the virtuous, no evil whatsoever would befall you. Since such a thing has befallen you, it cannot be that righteousness exists.
t.6.70.25: Or rather, dharma is weak and impotent, and it merely follows power. Something so weak, whose bounds have been swept away, is not worth following. That is my view.
t.6.70.26: If righteousness has become subordinate to might in matters of valor, then cast righteousness aside and conduct yourself in might just as you have in righteousness.
t.6.70.27: If indeed truthful speech is dharma, O scorcher of foes, then why did you not bind your father, who was false and pitiless toward you?
t.6.70.28: If dharma or adharma truly existed, O true one, O scorcher of foes, then Śatakratu, the wielder of the thunderbolt, would not have performed a sacrifice after slaying a sage.
t.6.70.29: Dharma, when it comes under the sway of adharma, brings about destruction, O Rāghava. A man does all this just as he pleases, O Kākutstha.
t.6.70.30: And this is my view, dear one, O Rāghava: you thought 'this is dharma,' yet when you gave up the kingdom back then, you cut off the very root of dharma.
t.6.70.31: For it is from wealth, grown great and gathered in from here and there, that all undertakings flow forth, just as rivers flow forth from the mountains.
t.6.70.32: For when a man of little vigour is bereft of wealth, all his undertakings are cut off, just as little streams dry up in the hot season.
t.6.70.34: He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen. He who has wealth is a man in the world, and he who has wealth is a learned man.
t.6.70.33: Such a man, having abandoned wealth, yet still longing for pleasure and raised in comfort, sets about doing evil, and in this way wrongdoing arises.
t.6.70.35: He who has wealth is valiant, and he who has wealth is wise; he who has wealth is highly fortunate, and he who has wealth is possessed of great virtues.
t.6.70.36: O hero, I have set forth these faults that lie in the abandonment of wealth, for it was you who, giving up the kingdom, made that resolve.
t.6.70.37: He who possesses wealth has dharma, kāma and artha, and for him everything turns out favorably. A man without wealth who longs for wealth cannot attain his object, however much he searches for it.
t.6.70.38: Joy, desire and pride, righteousness, anger, tranquility and self-restraint: all these arise from wealth, O lord of men.
t.6.70.39: Those riches, for want of which this world is lost to those who go about practicing dharma, are not to be seen in you, just as the planets are not seen on cloudy days.
t.6.70.40: O hero, when you had gone into exile and stood firm by the word of your father, your wife, dearer to you than your very life, was carried off by a rākṣasa.
t.6.70.41: Today, O hero, by my deeds I shall remove that great sorrow caused by Indrajit; therefore rise, O Rāghava.
t.6.70.42: O sinless one, here I am, having spoken this for your sake. Enraged at seeing the death of Janaka's daughter, I shall fiercely strike down with my arrows Laṅkā, together with its horses, elephants and chariots and with the lord of the rākṣasas.
